question: A licensee makes a substantial misrepresentation to a client, or makes false promises of a character likely to influence or induce a party to a transaction, or pursues a continued and flagrant course of misrepresentation (including through the acts of other licensees, employees, advertising, or otherwise). Under the disciplinary statute, this conduct is:
choice_a: Not disciplinable unless a court first finds common-law fraud
choice_b: Grounds for discipline, as one of the enumerated categories of misrepresentation-based violations
choice_c: Only actionable as a private civil claim, with no Commission jurisdiction
choice_d: Disciplinable only if the misrepresentation was in writing
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)'s opening subsections make substantial misrepresentation, false promises likely to influence a party, and a continued and flagrant course of misrepresentation (including through licensees, employees, or advertising) independently disciplinable grounds.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(a)-(c); hedge: exact (a)/(b)/(c) subsection boundaries not independently re-verified against primary leg.colorado.gov text this session (justia.com, casetext.com direct access, and dre.colorado.gov were blocked/403'd; only one casetext.com secondary-source summary succeeded) -- content reflects that summary plus standard misrepresentation/false-promise license-law framework.

question: A licensee's conduct in a real estate transaction violates the Colorado Consumer Protection Act. Under the real estate disciplinary statute, what effect does this have on the licensee's license?
choice_a: None -- the Real Estate Commission has no authority to act on Consumer Protection Act violations
choice_b: It is grounds for discipline only after a criminal conviction under the Act
choice_c: It is itself grounds for discipline under the real estate broker statute, separate from any Consumer Protection Act enforcement
choice_d: It automatically results in permanent revocation with no hearing
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(d) lists a licensee's violation of the Colorado Consumer Protection Act as an independent ground for discipline by the Commission.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(d); hedge: sourced via a single successful casetext.com secondary-source fetch -- primary leg.colorado.gov text was inaccessible this session (403/bot-detection on justia.com and dre.colorado.gov, and the leg.colorado.gov Title 12 PDF could not be text-extracted).

question: A broker performs licensed activities on behalf of another broker without that other broker's knowledge or consent. What is this?
choice_a: Permitted, as long as no fee is charged
choice_b: Permitted only between brokers within the same brokerage
choice_c: A civil matter only, outside Commission jurisdiction
choice_d: Grounds for discipline
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(f) makes it grounds for discipline for a licensee to act, or purport to act, as agent or representative of a broker without the knowledge and consent of that broker.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(f); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: A broker receives funds belonging to a client in connection with a real estate transaction but delays, without justification, in accounting for or remitting those funds. What does this constitute?
choice_a: Grounds for discipline for failing to account for or remit funds within a reasonable time
choice_b: A minor bookkeeping matter with no disciplinary exposure so long as the funds are eventually remitted
choice_c: Grounds for discipline only if the delay exceeds one full year
choice_d: A matter solely between the broker and the employing broker, not reportable to the Commission
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(h) makes it grounds for discipline to fail, within a reasonable time, to account for or remit any moneys coming into the licensee's possession that belong to another person.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(h); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: Beyond the specific acts individually enumerated, does the statute also make violating any provision of the real estate broker statutory scheme itself, or of a Commission rule or order, an independent ground for discipline?
choice_a: No -- only the specifically enumerated acts (misrepresentation, commingling, etc.) can support discipline
choice_b: Yes -- violating any provision of part 2 or article 10, or a rule or order of the Commission, is itself listed as a separate disciplinable ground
choice_c: Only if the violation also happens to be a crime
choice_d: Only if the Commission first amends its rules to say so
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(m) separately lists violating any provision of article 10 or a rule or order promulgated by the Commission as its own ground for discipline, distinct from the catch-all 'dishonest dealing' provision in (1)(w).
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(m); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: Aside from the requirement that a licensee immediately notify the Commission in writing of a qualifying conviction, is being convicted of, or pleading guilty or nolo contendere to, one of the statute's enumerated crimes itself an independent basis for discipline?
choice_a: No -- only the failure to report the conviction is disciplinable, not the underlying conviction
choice_b: Yes, but only for felony convictions occurring after licensure, never for pre-application convictions
choice_c: Yes -- conviction of, or a guilty/nolo plea to, one of the enumerated crimes (including certain Title 18 offenses) is itself listed as grounds for discipline, separate from the later notification duty
choice_d: No -- criminal convictions are handled exclusively by the courts and never affect licensure
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(n) itself lists conviction of, or a guilty or nolo contendere plea to, specified crimes (including certain offenses under Title 18) as grounds for discipline; the duty to immediately notify the Commission of such a conviction is a separate, later ground under (1)(p).
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(n); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: A licensee, in connection with a residential sale, refuses to show a home to a prospective buyer because of the buyer's race. Independent of any federal Fair Housing Act enforcement, does Colorado's real estate disciplinary statute treat this as grounds for discipline?
choice_a: No -- fair housing enforcement belongs exclusively to HUD and the courts, not the Real Estate Commission
choice_b: Only if the buyer first obtains a federal court judgment
choice_c: No -- the real estate statute only reaches financial misconduct, not discrimination
choice_d: Yes -- violating fair housing law is itself listed as a separate ground for discipline under the real estate broker statute
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(o) makes a licensee's violation of any applicable fair housing law an independent ground for Commission discipline, separate from any federal or other enforcement.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(o); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: A licensee's fraudulent conduct in a transaction results in a civil court entering a judgment against the licensee for fraud. Can this civil judgment itself, by statute, support real estate license discipline?
choice_a: Yes -- a civil judgment finding the licensee committed fraud is itself listed as an independent disciplinary ground
choice_b: No -- only a criminal fraud conviction can support discipline
choice_c: No -- civil judgments are confidential and unavailable to the Commission
choice_d: Yes, but only if the judgment exceeds $100,000
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(v) (added effective August 26, 2013, per the secondary source consulted) lists a licensee's fraud that results in a civil judgment against the licensee as an independent ground for discipline.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(v); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch, including the August 26, 2013 effective date; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session to independently confirm the effective date.

question: For how long does the statute require a licensee to maintain records evidencing completion of required continuing education, so that discipline can be imposed for failing to do so?
choice_a: One year
choice_b: Four years
choice_c: Ten years
choice_d: There is no record-retention requirement for continuing education
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(y) makes it grounds for discipline to fail to maintain records of completed continuing education for four years, mirroring the four-year retention period the statute separately applies to transaction records under (1)(k).
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(y); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: A licensee violates section 12-10-218 (which the disciplinary statute cross-references as its own separate ground for discipline). Beyond ordinary discipline, what additional monetary consequence does the statute authorize?
choice_a: A mandatory criminal fine of $10,000, set by the district attorney
choice_b: Automatic forfeiture of the licensee's entire real estate portfolio
choice_c: The Commission may assess a penalty equal to the amount of remuneration improperly paid or received in violation of that section
choice_d: No additional monetary consequence beyond the standard $2,500 per-offense fine
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(z) makes violating section 12-10-218 grounds for discipline and authorizes the Commission to assess a penalty equal to the amount of remuneration improperly paid, in addition to other available discipline.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(z); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch describing a penalty 'equal to improperly paid' remuneration; the underlying text of § 12-10-218 itself could not be independently retrieved this session.

question: A Colorado real estate licensee also holds a license as an insurance producer, and that insurance license is revoked in a separate disciplinary proceeding. Can this affect the licensee's real estate license?
choice_a: No -- discipline in an unrelated licensed profession can never affect a real estate license
choice_b: Yes, but only if the insurance revocation happened in Colorado and nowhere else
choice_c: No -- only revocation of another real estate license in another state counts
choice_d: Yes -- having a license revoked or suspended within the preceding five years in a related profession such as mortgage broker, appraiser, insurance producer, attorney, securities professional, or investment advisor is itself listed as grounds for real estate license discipline
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(aa) lists having had a license revoked or suspended within the preceding five years in a related field -- including mortgage broker, appraiser, insurance producer, attorney, securities professional, or investment advisor licensure -- as an independent ground for real estate license discipline.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(aa); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch, including the five-year window and the listed related professions; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: A rental location agent takes a fee from a prospective tenant in exchange for providing rental listing information. What must the agent provide under the statute?
choice_a: A contract or receipt that includes, among other things, the address and telephone number of the Commission
choice_b: Nothing -- rental location agents are exempt from all disclosure requirements
choice_c: A notarized copy of the agent's own real estate license
choice_d: A written appraisal of the rental unit's market value
explanation: Section 12-10-217(2) requires a rental location agent to furnish a contract or receipt to the person paying the fee, containing prescribed information including the Commission's address and telephone number.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(2); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: In connection with a Commission investigation, must a broker supply the Commission with copies of relevant legal documents and information about the disposition of related legal proceedings?
choice_a: No -- brokers may withhold any document subject to attorney-client privilege, even from the Commission
choice_b: Yes -- the statute requires a broker to supply the Commission with copies of such legal documents and information about case dispositions
choice_c: No -- only the broker's attorney may communicate with the Commission
choice_d: Yes, but only if a court first orders disclosure
explanation: Section 12-10-217(4) requires brokers to supply the Commission with copies of legal documents and information regarding the disposition of legal proceedings relevant to a Commission inquiry.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(4); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: If the Commission disciplines a licensee's real estate license for particular conduct, does that resolve the licensee's exposure to civil or criminal liability arising from the same conduct?
choice_a: Yes -- Commission discipline is the exclusive remedy and bars any later civil or criminal action
choice_b: Yes, but only as to civil liability; criminal liability is unaffected
choice_c: No -- the disciplinary statute does not relieve a licensee from civil or criminal liability for the same conduct
choice_d: Yes, but only as to criminal liability; civil liability is unaffected
explanation: Section 12-10-217(5) makes clear that administrative discipline under the statute does not relieve a licensee of separate civil or criminal liability arising from the same conduct.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(5); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: Where do administrative fines collected by the Commission under section 12-10-217 go?
choice_a: They are paid directly to the complaining party as restitution
choice_b: They are deposited into the state's general education fund
choice_c: They are returned to the disciplined licensee's employing broker
choice_d: They are transmitted to and become part of the Division of Real Estate's cash fund
explanation: Section 12-10-217(8) directs that administrative fines collected under the statute are transmitted to the Division of Real Estate's cash fund.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(8); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: A person's real estate broker license was revoked by the Colorado Real Estate Commission. Under the statute, how soon may that person apply for a new license?
choice_a: Not less than one year after the revocation
choice_b: Immediately, with no waiting period
choice_c: Not less than five years after the revocation
choice_d: Never -- a revoked applicant is permanently barred from reapplying
explanation: Section 12-10-217(9) requires an applicant whose license was revoked to wait at least one year from the date of revocation before applying for a new license.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(9); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: During a Commission investigation, the Division uncovers apparent evidence of criminal conduct by the licensee. What does the statute direct the Division to do with that evidence?
choice_a: Keep the evidence permanently confidential and take no further action
choice_b: Refer matters involving apparent criminal conduct to the appropriate law enforcement authorities
choice_c: Prosecute the criminal matter itself through Commission staff attorneys
choice_d: Destroy the evidence once the administrative case is closed
explanation: Section 12-10-217(10) directs the Division to refer matters involving apparent criminal conduct to the appropriate law enforcement authorities.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(10); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: Under the opening language of section 12-10-217(1), when is the Commission authorized to inquire into the conduct of a licensee?
choice_a: Only once per year, during license renewal
choice_b: Only after a criminal conviction has already occurred
choice_c: At any time, upon its own motion or on the complaint of any person
choice_d: Only within 30 days of the alleged conduct
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1) grants the Commission authority to inquire into the conduct of any licensee, or any person who assumes to act in that capacity, at any time, either on the Commission's own motion or on complaint.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1) intro; hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: Beyond an administrative fine, what range of other sanctions does the statute authorize the Commission to impose against a licensee found to have committed a disciplinable act?
choice_a: Only permanent revocation -- there is no intermediate sanction available
choice_b: Only a public reprimand, with no effect on licensure status
choice_c: Mandatory referral to the licensee's local board of REALTORS for private discipline
choice_d: Censure, probation, temporary suspension, or permanent revocation of the license
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1) authorizes the Commission, in addition to an administrative fine, to censure a licensee or to place the licensee on probation, or to temporarily suspend or permanently revoke the license.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session.

question: The Commission itself must not maintain a licensee's licensing history records for more than 7 years. Separately, a licensee must maintain the licensee's own prescribed transaction documents and records for a different, shorter period so they are available for Commission inspection. How long is that second period?
choice_a: 4 years -- distinct from, and shorter than, the Commission's own 7-year cap on retaining licensing history records
choice_b: 7 years, identical to the Commission's own record-retention cap
choice_c: 1 year
choice_d: There is no fixed period; the licensee may destroy records at will
explanation: Two separate retention rules exist: under section 12-10-216(2), the Commission need not preserve a licensee's licensing history records for more than 7 years, while under section 12-10-217(1)(k), the licensee must keep the licensee's own prescribed transaction documents and records for 4 years for Commission inspection.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. §§ 12-10-216(2), 12-10-217(1)(k) (comparison question); both underlying facts already appear individually in the original 23-question bucket and are treated as confirmed.

question: The statute contains two different 'catch-all' style grounds for discipline in subsection (1): one addressing violations of the statute or Commission rules generally, and another addressing dishonest dealing generally. How do these two catch-alls differ?
choice_a: They are identical in scope and either one alone would be redundant
choice_b: Subsection (m) reaches any violation of article 10 itself or of a Commission rule or order, while subsection (w) separately reaches any other conduct -- of the same or a different character than otherwise specified -- that constitutes dishonest dealing
choice_c: Subsection (m) applies only to brokers, while subsection (w) applies only to appraisers
choice_d: Subsection (w) applies only to criminal conduct, while subsection (m) applies only to civil conduct
explanation: Subsection (1)(m) is a catch-all for violating article 10 itself or a Commission rule or order, while subsection (1)(w) is a separate, broader catch-all for any other conduct -- whether or not otherwise specified in subsection (1) -- that amounts to dishonest dealing.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(m), (1)(w) (comparison question); (1)(w) already appears in the original 23-question bucket and is treated as confirmed, (1)(m) sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch.

question: A broker is found, after a single hearing, to have committed three separate, distinct violations of section 12-10-217(1) in the same transaction. Given that the maximum administrative fine is $2,500 per separate offense, what is the maximum total fine the Commission could impose for these three violations?
explanation: Because the $2,500 maximum fine under section 12-10-217(1) applies per separate offense, three distinct violations could support a maximum total fine of 3 x $2,500 = $7,500.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1) (application of the per-offense fine cap already confirmed in the original 23-question bucket).

question: A Colorado broker shares a commission on a cooperative sale with a person in a foreign country that does not license real estate brokers at all. Under the unlicensed-compensation exception, what must be true of that foreign person for the payment to be permitted?
choice_a: The person must hold a Colorado broker license as well
choice_b: The payment is never permitted if the foreign country does not license brokers
choice_c: The person must be a licensed attorney in that country
choice_d: The person must be a citizen or resident of that country and be in the business of selling real estate there
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(l)'s exception for paying an unlicensed person extends to a citizen or resident of a foreign country that does not license real estate brokers, provided that person is in the business of selling real estate in that country.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(l) (second exception clause; the first exception clause -- paying a broker licensed in another state or country -- already appears in the original 23-question bucket and is treated as confirmed).

question: A licensee's real estate license is suspended in another state for conduct that would NOT independently violate any provision of Colorado's own disciplinary subsection (1). Can the Colorado Commission discipline the licensee's Colorado license based solely on that out-of-state suspension?
choice_a: No -- the out-of-state action is only usable as a Colorado disciplinary ground if the underlying conduct would also constitute a violation of Colorado's subsection (1)
choice_b: Yes -- any out-of-state license suspension automatically triggers Colorado discipline, regardless of what the underlying conduct was
choice_c: No -- out-of-state disciplinary actions can never be considered by the Colorado Commission under any circumstance
choice_d: Yes, but only if the other state is adjacent to Colorado
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(x) only makes an out-of-state broker's or subdivision developer's license suspension or revocation a Colorado disciplinary ground if the underlying conduct would itself constitute a violation of Colorado's subsection (1) -- a bare out-of-state action on unrelated grounds is not, by itself, sufficient.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(x) (nuance -- underlying-conduct requirement -- on the same provision already present in the original 23-question bucket).

question: A newspaper reporter files an open-records request seeking the Commission's investigative file on a pending, unresolved complaint against a licensee. Must the Commission release the file?
choice_a: Yes -- all Commission records are public records subject to open-records requests
choice_b: No -- complaints of record and Commission investigations, including investigative files, are closed to public inspection while pending
choice_c: Yes, but only the licensee's name may be redacted
choice_d: No, but only if the licensee personally objects in writing
explanation: Section 12-10-217(6) closes complaints of record and Commission investigations, including investigative files, to public inspection; only stipulations and final agency orders are public records.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(6) (applied scenario on the confidentiality rule already present in the original 23-question bucket).

question: A broker temporarily uses funds held in the brokerage's escrow account to cover a shortfall in office payroll, intending to replace the money before any client needs it. Does the broker's intent to repay the funds prevent this from being a disciplinable act?
choice_a: Yes -- as long as the broker fully repays the escrow account within 30 days, no discipline can result
choice_b: Yes -- intent to repay is a complete statutory defense to any commingling charge
choice_c: No -- converting, diverting, or commingling funds of others with the broker's own funds is grounds for discipline regardless of any intent to repay
choice_d: No, but only if the shortfall exceeds $10,000
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(i) makes converting, diverting, or commingling funds of others with the broker's own funds grounds for discipline outright; the statute does not condition that violation on the broker's intent, or lack of intent, to later repay the funds.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(i) (scenario variant on the commingling ground already present once in the original 23-question bucket).

question: A listing broker refers the seller to a home inspector and, unknown to the seller, receives a referral fee from that inspector for the referral. Is this a disciplinable act even though the fee came from a third party rather than the seller?
choice_a: No -- the disclosure duty only applies to compensation paid by the broker's own client, not by third-party vendors
choice_b: No -- referral fees from home inspectors are categorically exempt from the disclosure requirement
choice_c: Yes, but only if the fee exceeds $500
choice_d: Yes -- claiming or taking secret or undisclosed compensation from any source, without revealing it to the principal, is grounds for discipline
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(t) makes it grounds for discipline to claim, arrange for, or take secret or undisclosed compensation or profit, or to fail to reveal to the principal the full amount of compensation the licensee receives -- including compensation from a third party such as a referred vendor.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(t) (scenario variant on the secret-compensation ground already present once in the original 23-question bucket).

question: A broker is simultaneously working with two different, competing prospective buyers who each want to submit an offer on the same listed property, without disclosing this dual representation to either buyer. Could this expose the broker to discipline for acting for more than one party without the knowledge of all parties?
choice_a: Yes -- the undisclosed multiple-representation ground applies to representing more than one party to a transaction without the knowledge of all of them, which can include two competing buyer-clients as well as a buyer and seller
choice_b: No -- the undisclosed multiple-representation ground applies only when one of the two parties is the seller
choice_c: No -- representing two buyers for the same listing is always permitted without any disclosure
choice_d: Yes, but only if the two buyers are related to each other
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(e) makes it grounds for discipline to act for more than one party to a transaction without the knowledge of all parties to it; that principle is not limited to a buyer-seller pairing and can extend to undisclosed representation of competing buyer-clients on the same property.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(e) (scenario variant on the undisclosed dual-representation ground already present once, in a buyer/seller framing, in the original 23-question bucket).

question: Two separate four-year record-retention duties appear in section 12-10-217(1): one for a licensee's transaction documents and records, and one for a licensee's continuing-education records. What do these two four-year duties have in common?
choice_a: Nothing -- one duty lasts four years and the other lasts seven years
choice_b: Both require the licensee, not the Commission, to keep the records available for Commission inspection for four years, and failing to do so under either is independently grounds for discipline
choice_c: Only the Commission, never the licensee, bears either retention duty
choice_d: Both duties were repealed and replaced by a single two-year rule
explanation: Section 12-10-217(1)(k) requires a licensee to keep prescribed transaction documents and records for four years for Commission inspection, and section 12-10-217(1)(y) separately requires a licensee to keep continuing-education completion records for four years; failing to comply with either is independently grounds for discipline.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(k), (1)(y) (comparison question); (1)(k) already appears in the original 23-question bucket and is treated as confirmed, (1)(y) sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch.

question: For the fraud-resulting-in-a-civil-judgment ground added to the disciplinary statute, is a mere allegation or lawsuit filing against the licensee, without more, sufficient to trigger this specific ground?
choice_a: Yes -- simply being named as a defendant in a fraud lawsuit is enough to trigger this ground
choice_b: Yes -- any settlement of a fraud claim, even without a judgment, automatically triggers this ground
choice_c: No -- this specific ground requires that the licensee's fraud actually resulted in a civil judgment being entered, not merely that a lawsuit alleging fraud was filed
choice_d: No -- this ground can never be triggered by any civil proceeding, only by a criminal conviction
explanation: As described by the secondary source consulted, section 12-10-217(1)(v) is framed around fraud that results in a civil judgment against the licensee -- an entered judgment, not merely the filing of an allegation or lawsuit.
source_note: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 12-10-217(1)(v); hedge: sourced via a single casetext.com secondary-source fetch describing this ground as 'fraud resulting in a civil judgment'; primary leg.colorado.gov text inaccessible this session to confirm the precise statutory phrasing.
